metadata.title: Effects of COVID-19 education policies on students’ learning proficiency in Latin America—Insights from PISA 2022

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2022 microdata for 10 Latin American countries and restricts the analytic sample to schools that were closed due to the pandemic, then merges student and school questionnaires. The authors report “weighted” and “unweighted” versions of ML evaluation metrics, but they do not name the specific PISA student/sampling weight variable(s) or any replicate-weight scheme in the provided text. Because the models are trained with scikit-learn/XGBoost and evaluated with both weighted and unweighted metrics, the manuscript suggests that some form of weighting was applied during evaluation, yet the exact weight variable is not documented here. For replication, analysts should use the official PISA 2022 sampling weights for student-level representativeness and include country fixed effects as done in the paper; if weights are not available in the ML pipeline, results should be interpreted as conditional on the modeling sample rather than fully population-representative.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Start from PISA 2022 student microdata for 11 LAC countries; exclude Costa Rica because ESCS is completely missing (6113 observations), then exclude remaining observations with missing ESCS, leaving 71,375 observations. Keep a set of student/family covariates (Table 1) and merge with the school dataset containing COVID-19 policy variables. Restrict the working sample to schools closed due to the pandemic (including cases where the school closure-day variable is missing: 7259 students), yielding 55,041 observations across 2358 schools. Outcomes are constructed by averaging the 10 plausible values for math and reading and then dichotomizing at PISA level-2 thresholds (math: 421; reading: 408). Missing covariates are imputed using KNN imputation (k=7) for the small proportion of missing data.

confounders_identified.variable_name: Teachers have time for digital devices

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2022 (15-year-olds) — Math achievement (binary: level 2 or above)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Gradient boosted trees (XGBoost) — Weighted: AUROC 0.8627, APRC 0.7261, ACC 0.8145, BACC 0.7503, F1 0.6474, MCC 0.5252; Unweighted: AUROC 0.8829, APRC 0.7707, ACC 0.8222, BACC 0.7713, F1 0.6846, MCC 0.5636. (Model comparison: GBT best; logit worst.)
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 (15-year-olds) math the study leveraged resources to support students, resources to support teachers, teacher communication with parents, number of days school closed, and socioeconomic status (ESCS) to predict math proficiency (level 2 or above), finding that gradient boosted trees (XGBoost) achieved the highest classification performance (e.g., weighted AUROC=0.8627) and that policy effects are non-linear and interact with closure duration (e.g., student resources show positive associations at medium/high CEP1 ranges, while teacher communication shows decreasing/negative tendencies at extended closures). This indicates that remote-learning policy packages should be designed with closure-length-dependent effectiveness in mind, prioritizing student-resource supports and connectivity-aligned investments to sustain math competency during prolonged shutdowns, while avoiding one-size-fits-all communication strategies.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2022 (15-year-olds) — Reading achievement (binary: level 2 or above)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Gradient boosted trees (XGBoost) — Weighted: AUROC 0.8497, APRC 0.8586, ACC 0.7641, BACC 0.7644, F1 0.7685, MCC 0.5284; Unweighted: AUROC 0.8690, APRC 0.8692, ACC 0.7817, BACC 0.7817, F1 0.7837, MCC 0.5634. (Model comparison: GBT best; logit worst.)
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 (15-year-olds) reading the study leveraged resources to support students, resources to support teachers, teacher communication with parents, number of days school closed, and family support for education to predict reading proficiency (level 2 or above), finding that gradient boosted trees (XGBoost) again outperformed logistic regression and neural networks (e.g., weighted AUROC=0.8497) and that policy–closure interactions are non-linear, with student-resource supports showing comparatively stronger positive associations for reading at longer closure durations. This indicates that reading recovery during pandemic shutdowns may be more responsive to sustained student-resource and engagement supports than to teacher-communication intensity alone, and that policy targeting should account for household educational support and closure length rather than relying on uniform remote-learning interventions.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2022 microdata for 10 Latin American countries (after excluding Costa Rica due to missing ESCS and restricting to schools closed during the pandemic), constructing binary outcomes for math and reading proficiency at PISA level 2 or above using averaged plausible values. It trains three binary classifiers—logistic regression, neural networks, and gradient boosted trees (XGBoost)—and selects the best model using AUROC in a 5-fold cross-validation with a holdout test set, while also using GroupKFold by school/country to reduce information leakage. For math, the best model is XGBoost with weighted AUROC=0.8627 and F1=0.6474; for reading, XGBoost reaches weighted AUROC=0.8497 and F1=0.7685. Explanations are produced with SHAP (TreeExplainer), showing non-linear policy effects and interactions with closure duration, but the authors emphasize the design is correlational (no causal claims). Missing covariates are imputed via KNN (k=7), and the manuscript reports weighted vs unweighted metrics without naming the exact weight variable, so representativeness and causal interpretation should be treated cautiously.
